Fireflies.ai Transcript

Title: Redwood Inference - pricing experiment follow-up + credits/overages walkthrough
Date: 2026-01-29
Time: 1:00 PM - 1:44 PM PT
Duration: 44 minutes

Attendees
- Jordan Blake (Redwood Inference)
- Cole Summers (Redwood Inference)
- Ava Chen (BrightWave Systems)
- Marco Ruiz (BrightWave Systems)
- Priya Desai (BrightWave Systems)

Summary (auto-generated)
BrightWave asked for clarity on Redwood’s current pricing experiment: how free credits are applied, how overage pricing works once credits are consumed, and what the source of truth is when console usage differs from invoice totals. Redwood explained credit application order, overage tiering, and common causes of console vs invoice deltas (time zone boundaries, rounding at aggregation, streaming partials, retries). Next steps include sharing a one-pager, sample invoice/console comparison, and a follow-up session to review exports and pilot sizing assumptions.

Topics (auto-generated)
- Pricing experiment: free credits + overage tiers
- How credits apply across chat/embeddings/rerank
- Console usage vs invoice totals (rounding, time zones, pending usage)
- Retries, streaming disconnects, caching/batching and what gets billed
- Pilot sizing + procurement questions

Action items (auto-generated)
- Redwood to send pricing/credits overage one-pager + example invoice
- BrightWave to send forecasted token usage and regions
- Schedule technical session on usage exports and metering

Questions (auto-generated)
- Do discounts stack with credits?
- Are retries billed? What about 429s/timeouts?
- Why does console sometimes show a different number than invoice?
- Are credits applied per workspace or per org?


Transcript

[00:00:03] Jordan Blake: Alright, I think we’re all here. Ava, Marco, Priya — good to see you again. This is the follow-up from the demo last week. You had a bunch of really specific questions on the pricing experiment and how credits and overages show up in the console versus the invoice.

[00:00:18] Ava Chen: Yep. Thanks for making time. Our finance team basically said, “We’re not approving a pilot unless we can reconcile what we see in-product with what gets billed.”

[00:00:27] Priya Desai: And also like, what’s the effective rate after credits. We got a little confused because the doc said “free credits monthly” but then in the UI it looked like it was per project.

[00:00:38] Jordan Blake: Totally fair. Cole is on with me — he owns a bunch of the billing hooks and quota logic — so he can go deeper on the metering side.

[00:00:46] Cole Summers: Hey everyone.

[00:00:48] Marco Ruiz: Hey.

[00:00:50] Jordan Blake: Quick agenda: first, I’ll restate the experiment structure we discussed. Second, we’ll do the credits and overage math with a concrete example. Third, we’ll talk through console versus invoice alignment, the “source of truth,” and what causes deltas. Then we’ll close with next steps.

[00:01:09] Ava Chen: Works.

[00:01:10] Priya Desai: Yep.

[00:01:12] Jordan Blake: Cool. So, you’re currently in the “H2-credits-overage-tiers” experiment cohort — meaning the offer has a monthly credit bucket, and then overage pricing kicks in at tiered rates after credits are exhausted. The important thing is the meter is still usage-based: tokens for chat/generation, embedding units for embeddings, and rerank units if you use reranking.

[00:01:33] Priya Desai: When you say “credit bucket,” is that like dollars or tokens?

[00:01:37] Jordan Blake: It’s denominated in dollars. So you get, say, $X in credits per month — those credits apply against eligible usage line items.

[00:01:46] Marco Ruiz: Eligible usage line items… so not everything?

[00:01:49] Jordan Blake: Right. In this experiment the credits apply to Hosted API usage: chat/completions tokens and embeddings. They do not apply to Dedicated commits — though you’re not on Dedicated right now — and they don’t apply to professional services.

[00:02:05] Ava Chen: So credits apply across endpoints, but only within Hosted.

[00:02:08] Jordan Blake: Exactly.

[00:02:11] Priya Desai: And is it per org? Because we have separate environments.

[00:02:15] Cole Summers: It’s per billing account, which for most customers maps to the org. If you have multiple projects/workspaces under the same billing account, they draw down from the same monthly credit pool.

[00:02:29] Priya Desai: Okay, good.

[00:02:31] Jordan Blake: Now the overage tiers. Once credits are exhausted, usage is priced per meter, and the experiment variant you’re in has lower rates after you cross a monthly spend threshold — basically volume discounts without needing a contract commit.

[00:02:49] Ava Chen: This is like the thing we do with AWS where the first chunk is expensive and it gets cheaper? Sort of.

[00:02:55] Jordan Blake: Similar shape, yes. And to be super explicit: credits apply first, then overages. Credits are not “tokens free then pay,” it’s “usage accumulates, credits offset dollars owed.”

[00:03:10] Marco Ruiz: Got it.

[00:03:12] Priya Desai: Are the credits like, “use it or lose it” monthly?

[00:03:16] Jordan Blake: In the experiment, yes, they reset each billing month; they don’t roll over.

[00:03:22] Ava Chen: Okay. Can we do an example? Because the rate cards always look simple until we try to tie it to token counts.

[00:03:29] Jordan Blake: Yep. Let’s do a made-up month. Let’s say you run 120 million total tokens through chat. And say the blended price for your tier comes out to $0.90 per million tokens — I’m using round numbers, not your exact quote.

[00:03:45] Priya Desai: Okay.

[00:03:46] Jordan Blake: That would be $108 of usage for chat tokens. If your monthly credit is, say, $50, the invoice would show $108 usage, minus $50 credits applied, net $58 for that portion.

[00:04:01] Ava Chen: And embeddings would be separate line item.

[00:04:03] Jordan Blake: Exactly, separate meter and line item.

[00:04:06] Marco Ruiz: Wait, so it still shows the gross usage and then a credit line, or does it just show net?

[00:04:11] Cole Summers: On the invoice we generally show line items for the meters, and then a credit/discount line item. In the console, depending on which view you’re on, you might see net spend or gross usage. That’s part of the confusion we’re trying to remove.

[00:04:27] Priya Desai: That’s… yeah, that’s what I saw. The console “Spend” number didn’t match the “Usage” tab totals.

[00:04:34] Cole Summers: Right. Spend can be net-of-credits in some screens, while Usage is always raw metered units. We’ll send screenshots of the exact places.

[00:04:43] Jordan Blake: Also you asked last time: do discounts stack with credits. In this experiment, credits stack with standard contractual discounts only if there’s a signed order form that specifies both. In self-serve, there’s no additional discount besides the experiment tiering.

[00:05:02] Priya Desai: So if we sign an enterprise contract later with, say, 10% off, credits still apply?

[00:05:08] Jordan Blake: Typically yes, but it depends on how the order form is structured. Most common is usage line items priced, then discount applied, then credits. We can confirm in writing for your legal team.

[00:05:21] Ava Chen: That’s important. We need that order: discount and then credit, or credit then discount. It changes the effective rate.

[00:05:28] Jordan Blake: Understood.

[00:05:30] Marco Ruiz: On the metering itself: is it input and output tokens billed separately?

[00:05:35] Cole Summers: For Hosted chat/generation, we track both prompt/input tokens and completion/output tokens. Pricing can be the same or different depending on plan, but metering records both. What the invoice shows is typically “total tokens” at the applicable rate for that model family, but we can provide the breakdown via exports.

[00:05:54] Marco Ruiz: If you do caching, like prompt caching, do those tokens count?

[00:05:59] Cole Summers: We record cached tokens as a dimension. Depending on the product setting, cached prompt tokens may be billed at a reduced rate or not billed. In your cohort right now, cached tokens are billed, but at a lower effective price. The console can show “cached vs uncached” if you enable that view.

[00:06:20] Ava Chen: That’s new to me. Our app will have a lot of repeated system prompts.

[00:06:24] Cole Summers: Yeah, so it matters. And batching: if we do continuous batching behind the scenes, you’re not billed for “batch overhead.” You’re billed for tokens generated/processed, not for GPU time.

[00:06:38] Priya Desai: But batching could change like, the number of requests. Are requests a billable meter?

[00:06:43] Jordan Blake: In your current plan, request count is not billed separately; it’s tracked for rate limiting and analytics.

[00:06:49] Priya Desai: Great.

[00:06:51] Ava Chen: Ok now the scary part: console versus invoice.

[00:06:55] Jordan Blake: Yep. Let’s do that.

[00:06:58] Cole Summers: So, first principle: invoice is produced from billing aggregates for a closed billing window. Console usage is near-real-time and can include pending late-arriving events. Usually that causes small deltas close to month end.

[00:07:13] Priya Desai: How late can events arrive?

[00:07:16] Cole Summers: Typically minutes. Worst case, hours, if there’s a downstream retry. But we don’t want it to be days.

[00:07:24] Marco Ruiz: And the console is showing UTC or local time?

[00:07:27] Cole Summers: Console usage graphs are normalized to UTC at the moment. Invoices are also based on UTC boundaries. But customers often compare to their own internal logs in local time, and that’s where “off by one day” comes from at month edges.

[00:07:45] Ava Chen: We are in Pacific time, and our internal billing month is basically calendar month in PT. So on the 31st at like 5pm, we’d already be in “next day” UTC.

[00:07:55] Cole Summers: Exactly.

[00:07:57] Priya Desai: But we also saw like, a 2-3% delta in a mid-month sample you sent. That’s not just time zones.

[00:08:06] Cole Summers: Right. The other big causes:
1) Rounding rules — whether rounding happens per-request or at the aggregated line item.
2) Streaming partials and disconnects — historically some vendors billed weirdly if a client disconnects.
3) Retries — whether tokens are counted twice if a request retries.

[00:08:29] Marco Ruiz: We do streaming a lot.

[00:08:31] Cole Summers: Yeah. In Redwood, for streaming, we bill only tokens that were actually generated and sent before the client disconnect, and we stop metering after disconnect.

[00:08:43] Ava Chen: “Stop metering after disconnect” is like the exact sentence our CFO asked for.

[00:08:48] Cole Summers: Yep. There’s still some nuance: if the model has already generated tokens server-side before we detect disconnect, we have to ensure those aren’t counted. We’ve improved that logic recently.

[00:09:04] Priya Desai: So there was a bug?

[00:09:06] Cole Summers: There was an edge case earlier in the quarter where disconnect detection could lag and we’d over-count by a small amount in some scenarios. That’s been addressed. For any impacted customers we did a backfill and credits as needed.

[00:09:23] Jordan Blake: To be clear, we’re not seeing that in current cohorts. And we’ll share the current documented behavior.

[00:09:30] Marco Ruiz: Okay. Retries: if we get a 429 and we retry, are we paying twice?

[00:09:36] Cole Summers: If the first attempt fails before tokens are generated, there should be zero tokens billed. If tokens were generated and the response failed mid-stream, then you’d be billed for tokens generated up to failure.

[00:09:50] Marco Ruiz: But if you retry and it succeeds, you might pay for the partial and the full?

[00:09:55] Cole Summers: Correct, because compute happened both times. That’s why we separate “request outcome” and “retry reason” in metering dimensions internally; it helps explain what happened.

[00:10:08] Ava Chen: Can we get that dimension in exports? Like so we can answer “why did we get charged for failed calls.”

[00:10:14] Cole Summers: Yes, via usage export we can include request_outcome and retry_reason as columns. There are some limits on cardinality, but the main buckets are there.

[00:10:26] Priya Desai: Okay, rounding rules. This is the one I couldn’t get an answer on last time. Do you round tokens per request? Or per day? Or per invoice?

[00:10:38] Cole Summers: Great question. Tokens themselves are integers, so the rounding mostly comes from pricing normalization — like pricing per 1K tokens or per 1M tokens. The documented behavior is that we aggregate raw token counts first for the invoice window, and then compute dollars. We do not round up each request independently.

[00:10:59] Priya Desai: That’s good.

[00:11:01] Ava Chen: Because rounding per request is like death by a thousand cuts.

[00:11:04] Cole Summers: Exactly.

[00:11:06] Marco Ruiz: But why would console and invoice differ then? If both are aggregating.

[00:11:11] Cole Summers: Console sometimes shows an estimated spend number that updates in near real time. If there’s late-arriving usage, or if model alias mapping changes (like “llama-3.1-70b” vs “llama3.1-70b” spelling), that can cause small mismatches until it’s normalized. Also, some views in console show token counts grouped by route/model, and invoice groups by billable SKU, which can roll up multiple model aliases.

[00:11:38] Ava Chen: So the invoice is grouped by SKU basically.

[00:11:41] Cole Summers: Right.

[00:11:43] Priya Desai: Another concern: credits. Do credits apply in real time or only when invoice is generated?

[00:11:49] Jordan Blake: Both. The console will show credit consumption through the month, but the invoice is final. If there’s a late adjustment, you might see a small difference until the month closes.

[00:12:03] Priya Desai: So spend might look higher mid-month if credits haven’t been applied yet?

[00:12:08] Cole Summers: Depends on the view. There’s “Usage” (units) and “Spend” (dollars). Spend should be net-of-credits in the billing account view, but the per-project drilldown can show gross. Again, we’ll show you where.

[00:12:25] Ava Chen: This is the kind of thing that creates tickets. Like, our engineers screenshot the project view and scream.

[00:12:31] Jordan Blake: Yep. We’ll give you an internal FAQ you can point them to.

[00:12:36] Marco Ruiz: Can we talk about overage tiers a bit more? Like what triggers a tier change? Is it tokens or dollars?

[00:12:44] Jordan Blake: In this experiment it’s based on monthly spend (pre-credits) in that billing month, per billing account. So once you cross threshold 1, the marginal rate decreases for additional usage.

[00:12:57] Priya Desai: Pre-credits is important.

[00:12:59] Jordan Blake: Exactly. Otherwise you get weird effects where credits prevent you from ever getting to the lower tier.

[00:13:06] Ava Chen: Does the tier apply retroactively to the whole month or just incremental?

[00:13:12] Jordan Blake: It’s incremental. So the first chunk is at tier 1, next chunk at tier 2. Like tax brackets.

[00:13:21] Priya Desai: Perfect.

[00:13:24] Marco Ruiz: And is this per model? We might use different models for different features.

[00:13:30] Jordan Blake: It’s at the account level, not per model, but pricing differs by model family. So you could have chat tokens on one model priced one way, embeddings another way.

[00:13:42] Marco Ruiz: Okay.

[00:13:44] Ava Chen: We also care about “overage pricing” in the sense of: if we set a budget, can we cap spend? Or do we have to build that ourselves.

[00:13:55] Cole Summers: You can set quotas/limits at the API key or project level. You can hard cap requests or tokens, or set alerts when spend crosses thresholds. For enterprise we can also do “soft cap + approval” workflows, but for self-serve it’s alerts and quotas.

[00:14:14] Ava Chen: That’s helpful.

[00:14:16] Priya Desai: And those quotas are based on… tokens counted in the same way as billing?

[00:14:21] Cole Summers: Yes, same metering events drive both quotas and billing aggregates. There can be minor timing differences — quotas are real-time, billing is batch — but the raw unit definition is consistent.

[00:14:38] Marco Ruiz: If we’re using streaming and we cut off early, does that help us control output tokens? Like do we only pay for what we saw.

[00:14:47] Cole Summers: You pay for generated tokens up to the cut-off. If you set max_tokens low or you stop the stream, that reduces billed output tokens.

[00:14:58] Ava Chen: Good.

[00:15:00] Jordan Blake: I want to hit the question you emailed: “How do we prove invoice lines tie to telemetry.” Cole, do you want to describe the mapping at a high level?

[00:15:10] Cole Summers: Sure. Each request emits telemetry with fields like: billing_account_id, project_id, model, region, endpoint_type (chat vs embeddings), and token counts. Those events roll up into daily and monthly aggregates. Invoice line items are generated from the monthly aggregates grouped by billable SKU dimensions: billing account, region, model family, endpoint type, and meter version.

[00:15:37] Priya Desai: Meter version?

[00:15:39] Cole Summers: Yeah. Basically we version meter definitions so if we ever change accounting rules (like streaming edge cases) it’s traceable. It shows up in exports.

[00:15:51] Ava Chen: That’s reassuring for audit.

[00:15:53] Marco Ruiz: Can we get access to raw events?

[00:15:56] Cole Summers: Not raw per-request events by default because of volume, but we can provide detailed exports aggregated by hour or day with the relevant dimensions. For some enterprise accounts we also support a streaming usage export to your data warehouse.

[00:16:12] Marco Ruiz: Okay.

[00:16:13] Ava Chen: I’m going to ask a procurement-ish question even though we’re not there yet. If we dispute an invoice, what’s the window?

[00:16:21] Jordan Blake: Standard is 30 days from invoice date for written notice. If we go to MSA, legal can negotiate, but that’s typical.

[00:16:30] Priya Desai: And what’s the mechanism? Like we open a ticket?

[00:16:33] Jordan Blake: Yep, you open a support ticket, and we’ll ask for request IDs and a date range, and we reconcile. If it’s on our side, we do a credit memo or apply credits.

[00:16:45] Marco Ruiz: Request IDs are available in headers?

[00:16:48] Cole Summers: Yes, in response headers and in the console logs view.

[00:16:54] Ava Chen: Great.

[00:16:56] Jordan Blake: Now, you mentioned last time you’re evaluating Bedrock and a couple others. Any differences on billing that you’re seeing there?

[00:17:04] Ava Chen: Honestly Bedrock is just hard to understand. It’s like model-specific pricing and then also AWS billing weirdness. OpenAI is simpler but we have data residency concerns.

[00:17:18] Priya Desai: And Anthropic direct is fine but we need consolidated billing across environments, which is why we’re looking at platforms.

[00:17:27] Jordan Blake: Makes sense. Our goal here is make it reconcilable.

[00:17:31] Marco Ruiz: Okay, can I ask about “overage” in the sense of, if we exceed the credit, do you ever throttle or does it just bill.

[00:17:39] Cole Summers: It just bills. Throttling is based on rate limits, not billing. But you can configure quotas to prevent accidental runaway.

[00:17:49] Marco Ruiz: Alright.

[00:17:51] Ava Chen: Can you walk us through what the console will show for the pilot? Like at day 10, day 20, etc.

[00:17:59] Jordan Blake: Yeah. So you’ll have a “Usage” page: you can filter by project, API key, model, region. It shows token totals, embeddings totals, and estimated spend. You’ll also see “Credits remaining” at the org billing view. As credits are consumed, it shows remaining balance.

[00:18:18] Priya Desai: Does it show “credits applied so far” or just remaining.

[00:18:22] Jordan Blake: Both, I believe. Cole?

[00:18:24] Cole Summers: Remaining and applied-to-date in the billing overview. Again, per-project pages might not show the credit line explicitly.

[00:18:36] Ava Chen: That’s okay as long as the billing overview is the source of truth.

[00:18:41] Cole Summers: For reconciling, yes.

[00:18:44] Marco Ruiz: What about multiple regions? We might have EU traffic later.

[00:18:49] Jordan Blake: Region appears as a dimension; pricing can vary by region depending on capacity costs. Invoices will break out by region if it’s material, otherwise it can roll up.

[00:19:03] Priya Desai: We’d need it broken out.

[00:19:05] Jordan Blake: Noted.

[00:19:07] Ava Chen: Another thing: We use a gateway that retries automatically. We want to avoid paying for retries caused by timeouts.

[00:19:16] Cole Summers: If timeouts happen after tokens were generated, you’d still pay for the generated tokens, because the model ran. But we can reduce those timeouts by tuning max_tokens, timeouts, and using the right region. Also, we can provide idempotency keys so if you retry the same request, we can dedupe in some cases — but not all, because generation is stochastic.

[00:19:41] Marco Ruiz: Do you support idempotency for chat completions?

[00:19:44] Cole Summers: For non-streaming responses, yes, with some constraints. For streaming it’s trickier.

[00:19:52] Ava Chen: Okay.

[00:19:54] Jordan Blake: Let’s shift to pilot sizing quickly, because credits/overage only matters if we understand your baseline usage. Ava, last time you said you’re starting with one feature.

[00:20:06] Ava Chen: Right. It’s a support assistant. Probably 2k concurrent users peak. The model would do maybe 1-2 calls per session, and we stream.

[00:20:18] Marco Ruiz: Average prompt maybe 1,200 tokens including context, output maybe 300-600 tokens depending.

[00:20:26] Priya Desai: Our finance wants a max exposure number per month.

[00:20:30] Jordan Blake: If you can send those assumptions (requests per day, average tokens, percent streaming), we can give you a conservative cost range and then we’ll configure quotas so you can’t exceed it.

[00:20:45] Ava Chen: Okay.

[00:20:47] Priya Desai: We also might do embeddings for search.

[00:20:50] Jordan Blake: Great. Embeddings are a separate meter. If it’s high volume, we’ll want to look at caching and batch sizes.

[00:20:59] Marco Ruiz: Do embeddings get credits too?

[00:21:02] Jordan Blake: In this experiment, yes. They count against the same $ credit pool.

[00:21:07] Priya Desai: So if we blow the whole credit on embeddings, chat would be overage.

[00:21:11] Jordan Blake: Correct.

[00:21:14] Ava Chen: That’s fine, we just need to see it.

[00:21:17] Cole Summers: In the usage breakdown, you’ll see by endpoint type.

[00:21:22] Marco Ruiz: You mentioned rerank units earlier. We don’t use rerank. But if we did, would it be on the same invoice.

[00:21:28] Jordan Blake: Yes, same invoice, separate line item.

[00:21:31] Ava Chen: Okay.

[00:21:33] Priya Desai: One more thing: do you have a “minimum invoice” or any platform fee?

[00:21:38] Jordan Blake: For self-serve Hosted, no minimum. For Dedicated and Private, there’s a commit/platform component.

[00:21:47] Ava Chen: We’re starting hosted.

[00:21:49] Jordan Blake: Yep.

[00:21:51] Marco Ruiz: When would we switch to Dedicated? Is it just cost.

[00:21:56] Jordan Blake: Usually when you want predictable throughput/latency and data isolation, or when cost at scale makes commit economics better. But not necessary for pilot.

[00:22:08] Ava Chen: Okay.

[00:22:10] Priya Desai: Coming back to reconciliation: if we export usage daily, can we tie it to invoice exactly? Like within 0.1%.

[00:22:19] Cole Summers: You should be able to tie within a small tolerance. The biggest sources of difference are (a) month boundary/time zone, (b) late-arriving events, and (c) if you’re comparing different groupings (model alias vs SKU). If you export for the exact invoice window in UTC and group by the invoice dimensions, it should match.

[00:22:42] Priya Desai: Okay.

[00:22:44] Ava Chen: Are there any known gotchas? Like “streaming partials are counted weird.”

[00:22:50] Cole Summers: The main gotcha historically is people assume “requests” are billed. They aren’t. It’s tokens. Another one is they compare to client-side tokenization which can differ from server-side tokenization for the model. So you should use the token counts Redwood returns, not your own tokenizer.

[00:23:12] Marco Ruiz: That’s a huge one. Because we use tiktoken.

[00:23:15] Cole Summers: Right. Different models, different tokenizers. Redwood’s meter uses the model’s tokenizer at time of request.

[00:23:24] Ava Chen: So on the response you return the token usage.

[00:23:27] Cole Summers: Yes — prompt_tokens, completion_tokens, total_tokens.

[00:23:31] Priya Desai: And that matches what’s billed.

[00:23:34] Cole Summers: That’s the intention, yes.

[00:23:37] Jordan Blake: We can share an example response payload if helpful.

[00:23:41] Ava Chen: Yeah.

[00:23:43] Jordan Blake: Priya, you asked about “per project credits.” Just to close that: it’s one credit pool per billing account.

[00:23:50] Priya Desai: Got it.

[00:23:52] Ava Chen: So what do we need from our side to start a pilot.

[00:23:56] Jordan Blake: Two things. First, confirm which plan we’re putting you on for the pilot — which is basically the experiment cohort already set up. Second, send your forecast so we set quotas and so your finance team isn’t surprised.

[00:24:11] Marco Ruiz: Is there anything special we need to do to ensure streaming usage is measured correctly.

[00:24:17] Cole Summers: No, it’s automatic. But best practice is: handle client disconnect cleanly, and if you cancel, send a cancel, don’t just drop the socket. Some SDKs do better than others.

[00:24:30] Marco Ruiz: Okay. We can do that.

[00:24:33] Ava Chen: We also have question about “free credits” and whether it requires a credit card.

[00:24:39] Jordan Blake: For self-serve, yes, you add a payment method. For enterprise pilot, we can do invoicing with net terms. But since you want a controlled pilot, we can start with invoicing if procurement needs it.

[00:24:55] Priya Desai: We can do card for pilot if there’s a hard cap.

[00:24:59] Jordan Blake: Great. We can set hard cap.

[00:25:02] Priya Desai: And then if we hit cap, what happens.

[00:25:05] Cole Summers: Requests will be rejected with quota exceeded. You can raise the cap manually.

[00:25:12] Ava Chen: Okay.

[00:25:13] Jordan Blake: I want to make sure we answered the “overage pricing” question: there’s no surprise overage beyond the defined tier rates. The only variance comes from your usage.

[00:25:26] Priya Desai: Right.

[00:25:28] Ava Chen: Can you send the tier table, but also like a sentence that says “tiers are incremental, thresholds based on pre-credit spend.”

[00:25:36] Jordan Blake: Yes. I’ll send that.

[00:25:40] Marco Ruiz: Do you support purchase of additional credits upfront? Like prepay.

[00:25:46] Jordan Blake: For enterprise, yes, we can do prepaid credits. In self-serve experiment, it’s monthly credits only.

[00:25:55] Priya Desai: Okay.

[00:25:56] Ava Chen: Another question from our internal folks: Is console spend excluding tax? Our invoices include VAT sometimes.

[00:26:05] Jordan Blake: Console spend is pre-tax. Taxes depend on billing address and tax status.

[00:26:10] Priya Desai: Great.

[00:26:12] Cole Summers: And console spend is an estimate until close.
